title: The icon corner
hookLine: Orthodox homes keep a beautiful corner for prayer

lines: A SHELF UP NEAR THE CEILING.
FACES ON WOOD, A LAMP IN RED GLASS.
cards: Up near the ceiling, in a living-room corner, a small shelf. On it, a few painted faces on wood: Christ, his mother, a saint or two. A little oil lamp flickers in red glass.
A dried palm branch is tucked behind one frame. On the other wall, the television; on the table, homework and keys. Nobody here built a chapel.
They gave one corner of an ordinary room a different job. Some Orthodox families pray before a shelf like this, morning and night.

teach.b: In Russian homes it has been called the beautiful corner, and other Orthodox families keep their own versions. Tradition puts it on the east wall where the room allows, toward the sunrise.
Icons of Christ and Mary sit there, often with the saints the family are named for. It's small on purpose: a shelf, not a shrine room.
Jesus, in the Sermon on the Mount: "But thou, when thou prayest, enter into thy closet, and when thou hast shut thy door, pray to thy Father which is in secret."
A closet there means an inner room; Jesus is warning against prayer put on for an audience. In a corner at home, nobody is watching but the faces on the shelf. Then, the habit.

teach.h: DANIEL'S WINDOW, THREE TIMES A DAY.
teach.b: In Daniel, a new law forbids prayer to anyone but the king, and Daniel goes home anyway: "his windows being open in his chamber toward Jerusalem, he kneeled upon his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did aforetime."
A room, a direction, a time, and a habit there before the trouble came. Last, Jacob, running from his brother, dreams of a ladder reaching to heaven.

He wakes and says, "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not," and, "this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." The icon corner says the same about a living room.
Other Christians keep their own versions: a Catholic home altar with a crucifix and a statue of Mary, or a chair by the window with a worn Bible on the arm. The shape changes; the idea holds.

how: Some Orthodox Christians keep an icon corner at home, with icons, a lamp and a prayer book, and pray there in the morning and evening; some Catholic families keep a home altar, and other Christians keep a quiet chair or shelf for prayer.

games.q: you're Daniel. a new law says anyone who prays to anyone but the king will be thrown to the lions. you go home. what do you do?
o: close the windows and pray where no one can see.
stop praying until the law changes.
open the windows toward Jerusalem and pray, as before.
games.why: he kneels at his open window three times a day, "as he did aforetime." the habit was there before the trouble came.

practice: Look around and choose one spot, a shelf, a windowsill, and in your mind clear it and set one thing there: a cross, an icon, a candle, a Bible, or a photo of someone you want to remember.
If you pray, you can pray there in your own words or your church's, the way Daniel kept his window; if you don't, let it be a corner kept for quiet.

wordCard.voice: The icon corner. A small place at home set apart for prayer, with icons, a lamp, and the things a family holds holy.

orig.note: Greek: an inner room or storeroom, the word behind "closet" in Matthew 6:6.

carryVoice: Your line: a corner of heaven. One small spot, kept for prayer. Until morning.
